prompt: An EXOTHERMIC reaction is one that…
options: gives out heat to the surroundings
takes in heat from the surroundings
explanation: Exothermic = energy released to the surroundings, so they warm up. (Endothermic = takes energy in, surroundings cool down.)
hint: Exo = exit — the energy leaves.

prompt: An ENDOTHERMIC reaction makes the surroundings…
explanation: Endothermic = energy taken IN from the surroundings, so the surroundings get colder.
hint: It takes energy in — where from?

prompt: Which of these is an exothermic process?
explanation: Combustion (burning a fuel) releases heat — exothermic. Photosynthesis, cold packs and electrolysis all take energy in.
hint: Which one gets hot?

prompt: Breaking a chemical bond…
explanation: Breaking bonds always absorbs energy (an endothermic step); making new bonds always releases energy (an exothermic step).
hint: You have to put energy IN to pull a bond apart.

prompt: Making a new chemical bond…
explanation: Making bonds releases energy (exothermic step); breaking bonds absorbs energy (endothermic step). The overall change is the balance of the two.
hint: Atoms 'snapping together' lets energy OUT.

prompt: On an energy-profile diagram for an EXOTHERMIC reaction, the products are drawn…
options: lower in energy than the reactants
at exactly the same energy as the reactants
higher in energy than the reactants
explanation: Exothermic: energy was released, so the products end up at a LOWER energy than the reactants.
hint: Energy left the system, so the products are lower down.

prompt: On an energy-profile diagram for an ENDOTHERMIC reaction, the products are drawn…
options: at the same level as the reactants
explanation: Endothermic: energy was taken in, so the products end up HIGHER in energy than the reactants.
hint: Energy was added to the system, so the products are higher up.

prompt: The 'hump' on an energy-profile diagram represents the…
options: activation energy — the minimum energy a collision needs to react
explanation: The barrier the reactants must get over is the activation energy; once past it, the reaction proceeds to the products.
hint: It's the 'hill' the reaction has to climb to get started.

prompt: Combustion, respiration and neutralisation are all…
options: neither — they involve no energy change
explanation: All three release energy to the surroundings — they're exothermic reactions.
hint: They all give out heat.

prompt: An 'instant cold pack' gets cold when a salt dissolves in water inside it. Dissolving that salt is therefore…
options: a chemical reaction that makes a gas
explanation: The pack cools down because the dissolving takes energy IN from the surroundings — an endothermic process.
hint: It gets cold — so energy is being absorbed.

prompt: A reaction is run in a polystyrene cup. The temperature of the mixture RISES. The reaction is…
explanation: A temperature rise means energy was released to the mixture — the reaction is exothermic.
hint: It got hotter — energy came OUT of the reaction.

prompt: Adding a catalyst changes an energy-profile diagram by…
options: lowering the activation-energy hump (but not moving the reactants or products)
explanation: A catalyst gives a lower-energy pathway, so the hump is smaller; the reactant and product energies (and ΔH) are unchanged.
hint: It makes the hill shorter — but the start and finish heights stay the same.

prompt: Why does a fuel often need a spark or flame to start burning, even though combustion is exothermic?
options: the spark cools the fuel down
the reaction still has an activation-energy barrier to get over before the energy starts coming out
explanation: Even exothermic reactions need enough energy to get over the activation-energy hump; the spark provides that initial push.
hint: There's still a 'hill' to climb before the downhill part.

prompt: Photosynthesis (plants making glucose from CO₂ and water using light) is…
options: a reaction with no energy change
explanation: Photosynthesis takes in energy (from sunlight) to build glucose — it's endothermic.
hint: It needs an energy source (the Sun) to happen.

prompt: Which sign of ΔH goes with an EXOTHERMIC reaction?
explanation: Exothermic releases energy, so ΔH is negative; endothermic absorbs energy, so ΔH is positive.
hint: Energy leaves the system → the energy change is negative.

prompt: A hand-warmer that works by iron slowly reacting with oxygen (rusting) is…
options: neither — rusting has no energy change
explanation: Oxidation reactions like rusting release heat — that's how the hand-warmer works. It's exothermic.
hint: It warms your hands — so it must be giving OUT heat.

prompt: A reaction releases 200 kJ when new bonds form but needed 150 kJ to break the old bonds. Overall, the reaction is…
options: exothermic, ΔH negative — more energy came out than went in
neither — the energy is exactly balanced
explanation: Out (200) > in (150), so there's a net release of 50 kJ — the reaction is exothermic.
hint: Compare the energy that came OUT with the energy that went IN.

prompt: A reaction needs 300 kJ to break bonds but only releases 250 kJ when new bonds form. The reaction is…
options: endothermic — more energy went in than came out
explanation: In (300) > out (250), so there's a net absorption of 50 kJ — the reaction is endothermic.
hint: Compare the energy in with the energy out — which is bigger?

prompt: Thermal decomposition (e.g. heating calcium carbonate to make calcium oxide + CO₂) is endothermic. This means…
options: it releases heat as it happens
it must be continuously heated to keep going (it takes energy in)
explanation: Endothermic reactions absorb energy; you have to keep supplying heat (e.g. a Bunsen flame) or the decomposition stops.
hint: You have to keep the heat ON for it to continue.

prompt: Two students mix an acid and an alkali in a cup and the temperature rises by 6 °C. They conclude the neutralisation is…
explanation: Temperature rose → energy released to the mixture → exothermic. Neutralisation reactions are exothermic.
hint: Rising temperature = exothermic.

prompt: On an energy-profile diagram, ΔH (the overall energy change) is the difference between…
options: the masses of the reactants and products
the height of the activation-energy hump and the reactants
the energy of the products and the energy of the reactants
explanation: ΔH = (energy of products) − (energy of reactants). Negative ⇒ exothermic (products lower); positive ⇒ endothermic (products higher).
hint: It's the vertical gap between where you START and where you FINISH.

prompt: Which statement about a catalyst on an energy-profile diagram is TRUE?
options: it lowers the activation energy but leaves ΔH unchanged
it removes the activation energy completely
explanation: A catalyst only lowers the activation-energy barrier; the start (reactants) and finish (products) energies — and so ΔH — are exactly the same.
hint: It changes the SIZE of the hill, not where the start and end points sit.

prompt: Why is it that 'every reaction is endothermic in its first step'?
options: because the reactants are always cold
this statement is false — no reaction breaks bonds
because all reactions cool the surroundings
because the first thing a reaction must do is BREAK existing bonds, and breaking bonds always absorbs energy
explanation: To rearrange atoms, a reaction must first break the old bonds (energy in); making new bonds (energy out) comes after. Whether it's exothermic OVERALL depends on which is bigger.
hint: What has to happen to the OLD bonds before new ones can form?

prompt: Burning methane, CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, is strongly exothermic. On its energy-profile diagram…
options: the products are well below the reactants
the products are well above the reactants
the products are level with the reactants
explanation: Exothermic + 'strongly' → the products sit well below the reactants on the diagram (a lot of energy was released); there's still a small hump (the spark needed to light it).
hint: Lots of energy out → the products end up a long way DOWN.

prompt: Which pair are BOTH endothermic?
options: photosynthesis and the thermal decomposition of a carbonate
explanation: Photosynthesis and thermal decomposition both take energy in. The others are all exothermic.
hint: Which two need an energy SUPPLY to happen?

prompt: If a reaction's energy-profile diagram shows the products HIGHER than the reactants, then during the reaction the surroundings…
explanation: Products higher = endothermic = energy was absorbed FROM the surroundings, so the surroundings cooled down.
hint: Energy went INTO the chemicals — where did it come from?

prompt: A catalyst speeds a reaction up. It does NOT…
options: get recovered for re-use at the end
change whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic
explanation: A catalyst can't change ΔH or which way the energy flows — it only lowers the activation-energy barrier so the reaction reaches the same end-point faster.
hint: Three of these a catalyst DOES do; one it can't.

prompt: Respiration in your cells (glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water) releases the energy that keeps you warm. Respiration is therefore…
explanation: Respiration releases energy (it's why you're warm) — an exothermic reaction, essentially a slow, controlled 'combustion' of glucose.
hint: It keeps you warm — so it gives OUT energy.

prompt: Electrolysis (splitting a compound using electricity, e.g. water → hydrogen + oxygen) is endothermic because…
options: it requires a continuous input of electrical energy to keep splitting the compound
explanation: Electrolysis must be driven by an energy supply (electricity); stop the current and it stops — the hallmark of an endothermic process.
hint: Cut the power and it stops — so it needs energy going IN.

prompt: A reaction profile has a tall activation-energy hump but the products are only slightly below the reactants. This reaction is…
options: exothermic but with a high activation energy, so it may need a strong 'push' to start
endothermic with a high activation energy
explanation: Products below reactants = exothermic; a tall hump = a high activation energy, so a big initial energy input (a strong spark/heat) is needed before the energy starts coming out.
hint: Products are lower (exo), but the hill in between is tall.

prompt: Balance the (exothermic) combustion of methane: __ CH₄ + __ O₂ → __ CO₂ + __ H₂O
explanation: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O — 1 C, 4 H and 4 O on each side. This releases a lot of energy — strongly exothermic.
hint: Balance C, then H (you'll need 2 H₂O), then count the oxygens on the right and match with O₂.

prompt: Balance the (exothermic) burning of hydrogen: __ H₂ + __ O₂ → __ H₂O
explanation: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O — 4 H and 2 O on each side. Hydrogen burning in oxygen is strongly exothermic.
hint: O₂ has 2 oxygens, so make 2 H₂O — then balance the hydrogen.

prompt: A reaction releases 400 kJ overall. The energy needed to break the reactant bonds was 600 kJ. How much energy was released when the new product bonds formed?
explanation: Energy released overall = (energy out from making bonds) − (energy in to break bonds). 400 = out − 600, so out = 1000 kJ.
hint: Out − In = the overall release; rearrange to find 'out'.

prompt: Two reactions, A and B, have the same reactants and the same products, but B is run with a catalyst. Which statement is true?
options: B has a smaller ΔH than A
A and B have the same ΔH; only B's activation energy is lower
B is exothermic while A is endothermic
B makes more product than A
explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy but doesn't touch the reactant or product energies — same start, same finish, same ΔH; just a smaller barrier and a faster reaction.
hint: ΔH depends only on the start and end points — does the catalyst move those?

prompt: On an energy-profile diagram, the activation energy is measured from…
options: the reactants up to the top of the hump
the top of the hump down to the products
the room temperature up to the products
the products up to the top of the hump
explanation: The activation energy is the energy gap between the reactants and the peak of the hump — the energy a collision needs to start the reaction.
hint: Start at the REACTANTS — how far up is the top of the hill?

prompt: Why does a 'self-heating' food can (which uses an exothermic reaction) NOT need to be heated first to work?
options: exothermic reactions always start on their own
the reaction releases energy as it goes, and its activation energy is low enough that just mixing the reactants starts it
the can is already hot in the shop
explanation: It's exothermic (releases energy) AND has a low enough activation energy that bringing the reactants together gets it going — no external heat needed, unlike a Bunsen-flame-needing combustion.
hint: Two things matter: which way the energy flows, AND how big the starting hill is.

prompt: A polystyrene cup is used instead of a glass beaker for measuring a reaction's temperature change because polystyrene…
options: is a poor conductor, so less heat escapes to (or enters from) the surroundings — giving a truer temperature change
explanation: Polystyrene insulates well, minimising heat exchange with the room, so the measured temperature change more accurately reflects the reaction's energy change.
hint: You want to keep the heat IN (or out) so your reading is fair — what property does that?

prompt: Hydrogen is studied as a fuel: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Compared with the energy needed to break the bonds (in H₂ and O₂), the energy released when the new bonds (in H₂O) form…
options: is exactly equal, so ΔH is zero
is zero — no energy is released
is less, so the reaction is endothermic
is more, so the reaction is exothermic — a net release of energy
explanation: Burning hydrogen is exothermic, so making the O–H bonds in water releases more energy than was absorbed breaking the H–H and O=O bonds — a net release.
hint: Burning hydrogen gives out heat — so which step 'wins', breaking or making?

prompt: Which of these would NOT change ΔH for a given reaction?
options: the reaction not happening at all
doing the reaction with completely different reactants
explanation: ΔH is fixed by the reactants and products; a catalyst changes only the route (and so the rate), not the start and end energies. Different reactants or products would give a different ΔH.
hint: ΔH depends on the start and end states — which option doesn't change those?

prompt: A reaction profile shows: reactants at energy 50, peak at 90, products at 30 (arbitrary units). The activation energy and the type of reaction are…
explanation: Activation energy = peak − reactants = 90 − 50 = 40. Products (30) are below reactants (50) → energy was released → exothermic.
hint: Activation energy = peak minus reactants; exo/endo from where the products sit versus the reactants.

prompt: Why is 'a reaction is exothermic' not enough on its own to guarantee it happens quickly at room temperature?
options: exothermic reactions only happen when cooled
it might have a high activation energy — a big barrier to get over before the energy is released — so it can be very slow without a spark or catalyst
explanation: ΔH (exo/endo) tells you the OVERALL energy direction, but the activation energy controls how easily the reaction starts; a high barrier means a slow (or stalled) reaction even though it's exothermic.
hint: Energy direction is one thing; the size of the starting hill is another.

prompt: A student claims 'adding a catalyst makes the reaction give out more heat'. Why is this wrong?
options: ΔH — the heat given out (or taken in) per amount reacted — is set by the reactants and products; a catalyst only speeds the reaction up, so the same total heat comes out, just faster
catalysts are used up, so they add their own heat
explanation: The total energy change depends only on what reacts and what's formed; a catalyst changes the speed (the activation energy), not the amount of energy released.
hint: Faster ≠ more energy — the total heat is fixed by the reactants and products.

prompt: In an exothermic reaction run in an open beaker, where does the released energy mostly go?
options: it heats up the reaction mixture and then the surroundings (the air, the beaker, the bench)
it is stored in the products as extra bonds
explanation: The energy released warms the mixture, then spreads out into the surroundings — which is exactly why the surroundings get warmer for an exothermic reaction.
hint: If the surroundings get warmer, the energy went... where?

prompt: Two reactions both convert reactants at energy 60 to products at energy 20. Reaction X has a peak at 100; reaction Y has a peak at 75. Which is faster (at the same temperature), and do they have the same ΔH?
options: they are equally fast; different ΔH
Y is faster; same ΔH (both ΔH = −40)
explanation: Y has the lower activation energy (75 − 60 = 15, versus 100 − 60 = 40), so Y is faster; both go from 60 to 20, so both have ΔH = −40 (exothermic) — same ΔH, different barrier.
hint: Lower hump = faster; ΔH depends only on the start (60) and the end (20).

prompt: Balance the (endothermic) thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate: __ CaCO₃ → __ CaO + __ CO₂
explanation: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ — already 1:1:1; 1 Ca, 1 C and 3 O on each side. It must be kept hot — an endothermic reaction.
hint: Count each element — a thermal-decomposition equation is sometimes already balanced as written.
